basic_information.short_title: General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro, FY 2025
basic_information.official_title: AN ACT APPROPRIATING FUNDS FOR THE OPERATION OF THE BANGSAMORO GOVERNMENT FROM JANUARY ONE TO DECEMBER THIRTY-ONE, TWO THOUSAND AND TWENTY-FIVE AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES

citizen_summary.what_is_this_about: The region's ₱94.41 billion budget for 2025 — the only Bangsamoro budget that is smaller than the one before it, and the first to write the Province of Sulu's departure into its general provisions.
citizen_summary.why_was_it_proposed: The Bangsamoro Government requires an annual appropriations act to operate. This one covers 1 January to 31 December 2025 and carries the same theme as the year before, “Accelerating Structural Reforms, Boosting Sustainable Development, and Enhancing Human Capital in the Bangsamoro”.
citizen_summary.what_will_change: ₱94,411,666,856.24 is appropriated from the annual block grant, other subsidies from the National Government, the region's share of national taxes, fees and charges collected in its territory, and other revenues. The act funds 17 ministries, 11 other executive offices and 7 special purpose funds, and carries 76 sections of general provisions.
who_will_be_affected: Everyone in the region, through the ministries and services this funds
The people of Sulu, whose programmes and personnel this act continues to fund
Constituent local government units, through a ₱10.15 billion support fund
All Bangsamoro Government personnel, through a new medical allowance
Government lawyers, through a new special counsel allowance
Contractors and suppliers, through procurement and disclosure rules

what_this_means_for_you.in_short: This is a money law: it decides how much funding BARMM ministries and programs get - the schools, hospitals, roads, scholarships, and social services you use are all paid from it. No single citizen 'applies' for it, but nearly every public service you touch depends on it.
in_practice: Sets each ministry's budget ceiling for the year (or adds/extends funds mid-year for supplementals and extensions)
Slow disbursement is the recurring issue - several BAAs exist purely to extend the validity of unspent funds
Big-ticket items to watch: education (MBHTE), health (MOH), public works (MPW), and the Special Development Fund for conflict-affected communities

for_specific_groups.Parents & students: Classroom construction, teacher hiring, and scholarship slots are set here
for_specific_groups.Patients: Hospital operating budgets, medicines, and health worker salaries flow from this law
for_specific_groups.Workers & suppliers: Government projects and procurement opportunities follow the appropriations
for_specific_groups.Taxpayers: This is the accountability document - compare what was appropriated with what was actually delivered

watch_out_for: A law appropriating funds is a promise on paper: actual services depend on the budget being released and spent - ask the implementing ministry for the implementation timeline.
Follow-up reports: the Parliament itself has passed resolutions demanding ministries account for these funds
what_this_means_for_you.when_you_will_feel_it: Laws take effect shortly after publication, but felt impact follows budgets, IRRs, and agency rollout - typically months, not days
what_you_can_do: Ask your municipal/barangay office or the implementing ministry how and when it will roll out where you live
Read the full text (PDF) on the Parliament's website or the Official Gazette of the Bangsamoro - the final sections say when it takes effect and who must act
If it isn't being implemented, raise it with your Member of Parliament or through the ministry's public assistance desk

key_terms_explained.BAA: Bangsamoro Autonomy Act - a regional law passed by the Bangsamoro Parliament, applying inside BARMM alongside national laws.
key_terms_explained.IRR: Implementing Rules and Regulations - the ministry-issued 'how-to' that turns a law's text into procedures; many laws only bite once the IRR is out.
key_terms_explained.GAA: General Appropriations Act - the annual budget law deciding how much each ministry and program gets.

benefits.headline: Funds every public service you use - the enabler of all other benefits.

direct_benefits.benefit: Operating budgets for schools, hospitals, roads, scholarships, social programs
Salaries of teachers, health workers, and government personnel
Special Development Fund projects in conflict-affected communities

indirect_benefits: Procurement and job opportunities from funded projects
Predictability: agencies can plan the year
limitations: Benefits arrive only as fast as funds are released and the implementing office organizes - expect a lag between enactment and service.
Compare appropriations vs. actual delivery - Parliament's own resolutions demand these reports; you can too

key_provisions: Section 1 — Appropriation of Funds. ₱94,411,666,856.24 is appropriated “out of the annual block grant, other subsidies from the National Government, share in the National Government taxes, fees and charges collected in the Bangsamoro territorial jurisdiction, and other revenues” for the operation of the Bangsamoro Government from 1 January to 31 December 2025. The FY 2024 act had itemised two further sources — unutilized prior years' appropriations and unutilized prior year's allotments reverted to the Treasury; here they are folded into the open-ended phrase “and other revenues”. The total is 4.1% lower than FY 2024, the only year-on-year fall in the series.

Bangsamoro Government Budget — The act funds 17 ministries and 11 other executive offices. The Bangsamoro Transition Authority receives ₱5,330,726,658.00, or 5.6% of the total — its highest share to that point: General Administration and Support ₱833,233,604, Support to Operations ₱544,192,015 and Operations ₱3,953,301,039. Within Operations sit a Legislation Program of ₱1,606,101,039, a Representation Program of ₱1,654,656,000, an Oversight Program of ₱384,544,000, a Constituency Servicing Program of ₱288,000,000 and a Philippine Congress–Bangsamoro Parliament Forum of ₱20,000,000. Its object-of-expenditure schedule lists Representation Expenses of ₱1,422,560,744, Professional Services ₱414,321,521, Financial Assistance/Subsidy ₱361,700,000 and Traveling Expenses ₱350,165,429.

Special purpose funds — 7 funds, up from 6. The Local Government Support Fund rises to ₱10,153,071,200.00 — 10.8% of the whole budget and the largest special purpose fund by a wide margin. The Special Development Fund holds at ₱5,000,000,000.00. The Miscellaneous Personnel Benefit Fund is ₱2,164,833,311.00 and the Pension and Gratuity Fund ₱1,720,911,583.00, roughly 4 times its FY 2024 level. The Contingent Fund falls to ₱666,798,436.24 — 0.7% of the budget, against 20.0% in FY 2020 — and again carries a “provision for cost of acquisition of Al-Amanah Islamic Bank and other related costs” alongside funding for Islamic finance programmes under Section 29. Two funds are new: a Bangsamoro Shari'ah Court Support Fund of ₱27,480,000.00 and a Bangsamoro Under Special Circumstances Support Fund of ₱500,000,000.00.

Sections 2–15 (Receipts and Income) — The act itself serves as the allotment order except for appropriations with pre-release conditions and lump sums without release details. Fees, charges and revenues are remitted to the Bangsamoro Treasury under Section 3, Chapter I, Book VII of BAA 13, with exceptions: hospitals and health facilities remit 20% of income generated, motorised banca registration and licensing 50%, seaport charges 60%, and radio station licences and permits 60%, each under Title XV, Book VI of the same code. Foreign grants require prior clearance from the President and follow the Intergovernmental Fiscal Policy Board's Guidelines on Foreign Grants approved 5 February 2021. Section 7 brings public-private partnership receipts under RA 11966, the PPP Code of the Philippines. Section 10, new this year, authorises the Chief Minister on the finance minister's recommendation to invest idle funds in excess of normal operating requirements in treasury bills through the Bureau of the Treasury, subject to Parliament's approval through the Committee on Finance, Budget and Management, with a quarterly report due within 7 days of each quarter's end. Section 11 requires the Treasury to publish, on the finance ministry's website, the agency, funding source, legal basis and allowable uses of every Special Account and Fund, and requires agency posts to be searchable. Section 15 governs loans and Official Development Assistance under Section 24, Article XII of RA 11054 and the Intergovernmental Fiscal Policy Board's ODA guidelines approved 3 September 2024.

Sections 16–25 (Expenditure) — Procurement follows existing government procurement law, and Section 17 makes the Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System “the primary source of information and channel in the conduct of all procurement activities of the government” — the first time a Bangsamoro budget names it. Early procurement is authorised up to award, common-use supplies come from the Procurement Service, and supply inventories are capped at a 3-month requirement, with purchases beyond a 1-year requirement needing the Chief Minister's approval. Electric vehicle purchases must comply with RA 11697. No official may be sent to foreign training if due to retire within 1 year of the travel. Infrastructure projects may not be sited in critical geohazard areas or no-build zones, must meet the structural strength and climate resilience standards set by the Ministry of Public Works, and must minimise biodiversity loss within the National Integrated Protected Area System; engineering and administrative overhead is capped at 1% of project funds for projects over ₱1,000,000. Rainwater collection systems are required in public markets, school sites and government buildings, and may never be built on private lots. A Certification of Availability of Funds is required before any obligation, and a Multi-Year Contractual Authority before any multi-year contract.

Section 30 — Programs and Projects Intended for the Province of Sulu. Programmes, projects and activities intended for Sulu and funded under the budgets of the different agencies “shall continue to be implemented by them, as contemplated in the 26 November 2024 Supreme Court Resolution on the Motions for Reconsideration in the Case of Province of Sulu, et. al, versus Executive Secretary Medialdea (G.R. No. 242255), where it says that ‘appropriate mechanisms must be applied to validate, adapt, or conclude these projects and programs in a way that minimizes potential disruptions to the public interest, maintains stability, and protects the welfare of the people of Sulu.’” Personnel necessary to implement them “shall continue to be funded by the M/O/As, as appropriated herein”. Meanwhile the agencies, their National Government counterparts and the provincial and municipal governments of Sulu “shall design a Transition Plan towards implementing the Supreme Court Decision”, subject to agreements made in the Intergovernmental Relations Body.

Sections 26–35 (Other cross-cutting programmes) — Every agency must formulate a Gender and Development Plan integrated into its regular activities amounting to at least 5% of its budget, following RA 9710, with plans and accomplishment reports submitted under Bangsamoro Women Commission guidelines and feeding a Gender Financing Framework. Agencies must address senior citizens and persons with disability, and all government infrastructure must include accessibility features. Youth projects should align with the Philippine Youth Development Plan 2023–2028. Section 29 continues the direction to mainstream Islamic or Shari'ah-compliant finance. Built heritage and cultural landscapes may be altered only with the Chief Minister's prior approval after recommendation of the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage. All projects must be subjected to multi-scenario, probabilistic risk analysis, with technical assistance from the Bangsamoro Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council; agencies must assess their organisational carbon footprint, adopt energy-efficient lighting and inverter air-conditioning, protect biodiversity, and retrofit structures in seismically vulnerable areas.

Sections 36–52 (Personnel benefits) — Section 36 caps Personnel Services for one fiscal year at 45% of the Bangsamoro Government's total revenue sources, under Section 6, Article XII of RA 11054. Section 38 sets annual extraordinary expenses at ₱264,000 for the Chief Minister, ₱108,000 for each Deputy Chief Minister, the Speaker and each Member of the Parliament, ₱45,600 for each Minister, ₱26,400 for each Deputy Minister or Bangsamoro Director-General and ₱19,200 for each Director II or Director III, with miscellaneous expenses of up to ₱90,000 for each of their offices, and expressly bars using any of it for salaries, allowances or confidential and intelligence expenses. Section 42 keeps the ₱5,000 floor under monthly net take-home pay; Section 43 keeps PERA at ₱2,000 a month; Section 44 keeps the uniform or clothing allowance at ₱7,000 a year. Section 45, new this year, adds a medical allowance of up to ₱7,000 a year for HMO-type benefits. Section 47, also new, grants Bangsamoro government lawyers ₱5,000 for each court appearance, provided the appearance is not for a motion for extension or postponement and the monthly total does not exceed 50% of the lawyer's basic salary — and provides that “in no case shall special counsel allowance be granted to government lawyers appearing before quasi-judicial and administrative agencies”. Section 48 limits honoraria to a defined list, capping special-project honoraria at 25% of annual basic salaries. Section 49 keeps representation and transportation allowances at ₱15,500 for the Chief Minister, ₱12,500 for Deputy Chief Ministers, the Speaker and Members of the Parliament, ₱10,000 for Ministers, ₱9,500 for Deputy Ministers, ₱8,500 for Director II and Director III and ₱6,000 for Chiefs of Division and Director I, and invalidates any prior administrative authorisation inconsistent with those rates. Sections 50 and 51 grant a mid-year bonus of 1 month's basic salary and a year-end bonus of 1 month plus a ₱5,000 cash gift.

Sections 53–66 (Release and use of funds) — Section 53 makes appropriations available for release and disbursement until 31 December 2026, with Personnel Services valid only to 31 December 2025. After the validity period all unreleased appropriations, unobligated allotments and obligated allotments for goods, services or projects not yet delivered or completed revert to the Bangsamoro Treasury under a Special Fund for reappropriation under Section 19, Article XII of RA 11054. The constituent LGUs' share in taxes, fees and charges collected within the region “shall be available until fully released, obligated, and disbursed” — it does not lapse. Funds transferred between organisational units, between agencies or to local government units are not considered disbursed until actually used. Section 54 restores the heading “Prohibition Against Retention or Deduction of Funds” and, for the first time in any Bangsamoro budget, the operative sentence: “No retention or deduction as reserves or overhead shall be made, except as authorized by law, the general or special provisions in this Act.” Only the Chief Minister and the Speaker may declare and use savings, and only to augment actual deficiencies in existing items of their own appropriations, with semestral and annual reports on savings to be submitted to Parliament and posted on their websites. A discontinued or abandoned programme used as the basis for declaring savings may not be proposed for funding for the next 2 fiscal years. Cash advances may not be granted until earlier ones are liquidated, and an Annual Report on Cash Advances naming the recipients must go to the Committee on Finance, and Budget and Management.

Sections 67–77 (Administrative procedures and final provisions) — Ministers must review their mandates and identify functions that could be scaled down, phased out or abolished, and the Chief Minister may create offices, modify structures and create or reclassify positions within the appropriations authorised. Foreign travel of Ministers, Heads of Offices or Agencies and officials at salary grade 25 and above requires clearance from the Office of the Chief Minister. Section 71 requires a status report to the Commission on Audit within 60 days of receiving its Annual Audit Report. Section 72 requires financial and physical accountability reports, with failure resulting in “the automatic suspension of the salaries of the responsible official or employee until they have complied”. Section 73 requires publication of each infrastructure project's title, location, description, estimates, winning contractor and bid within 30 calendar days of contract, and of its detailed actual cost and any variation orders within 30 calendar days of the certificate of completion, and directs the Regional Project Monitoring and Evaluation Committee to promulgate guidelines requiring agencies to report status and percentage of completion on an official website they must establish and maintain. Section 74 cautions any court or agency against garnishing or subjecting public funds to levy and execution. Section 75 makes payment for the Personnel Services of employees absorbed under Section 10, Article XVI of RA 11054 without prejudice to a funding request to the National Government. Section 77 sets effectivity at 1 January 2025.

impact.figures_note: Grand total quoted from Section 1 — 4.1% lower than FY 2024, the only fall in the series. related_legislation.related_note: BAA 75, the FY 2025 Supplemental Appropriations Act, added ₱11,300,000,000 in May 2025, funded from previously unspent money. Funding sources and the 45% Personnel Services ceiling derive from Sections 6, 19 and 24 of Article XII of RA 11054, the Organic Law; the ₱5 billion annual Special Development Fund comes from Article XIV. Remittance of agency income follows Book VII of BAA 13, the Bangsamoro Administrative Code, with retention rates from its Title XV, Book VI. Public-private partnership receipts follow RA 11966, the PPP Code of the Philippines, and electric vehicle purchases RA 11697. Section 30 gives effect to the Supreme Court's Resolution of 26 November 2024 in Province of Sulu v. Executive Secretary Medialdea (G.R. No. 242255); the FY 2026 act's Section 29 later takes the matter further, citing Executive Order No. 91 declaring Sulu part of Region IX. Gender and development follows RA 9710 and reports flow to the Bangsamoro Women Commission created by BAA 8. BAA 84, the Bangsamoro Budget System Act of 2025, codifies as permanent law many of the rules this act carries annually.

citizen_questions.q: How big was the 2025 regional budget?
citizen_questions.a: ₱94,411,666,856.24, covering 1 January to 31 December 2025 — 4.1% less than FY 2024. It is the only Bangsamoro budget smaller than the one before it. BAA 75 later added ₱11,300,000,000 in supplemental funds.

citizen_questions.q: Where did the money come from?
citizen_questions.a: The annual block grant, other subsidies from the National Government, the region's share of national taxes, fees and charges collected in its territory, “and other revenues”. The FY 2024 act had named unutilized prior years' appropriations and reverted allotments explicitly; this one folds them into an open-ended phrase.

citizen_questions.q: What does the act say about Sulu?
citizen_questions.a: Section 30 provides that programmes, projects and activities intended for the Province of Sulu funded under the agencies' budgets “shall continue to be implemented by them”, as contemplated in the Supreme Court's Resolution of 26 November 2024 in Province of Sulu v. Executive Secretary Medialdea, which said that “appropriate mechanisms must be applied to validate, adapt, or conclude these projects and programs in a way that minimizes potential disruptions to the public interest, maintains stability, and protects the welfare of the people of Sulu”. The personnel needed to implement them stay funded, and the agencies, their national counterparts and the Sulu local governments are to design a Transition Plan through the Intergovernmental Relations Body.

₱5,330,726,658 through the Bangsamoro Transition Authority — 5.6% of the whole budget, its largest share to that point. Within it sit a Representation Program of ₱1,654,656,000, a Legislation Program of ₱1,606,101,039, an Oversight Program of ₱384,544,000, a Constituency Servicing Program of ₱288,000,000 and a Philippine Congress–Bangsamoro Parliament Forum of ₱20,000,000.

A Local Government Support Fund of ₱10,153,071,200 — 10.8% of the budget and the largest special purpose fund by a wide margin, up from ₱6.54 billion the year before. Their share of taxes collected within the region does not lapse: under Section 53 it stays available “until fully released, obligated, and disbursed”.

citizen_questions.q: What new allowances did employees get?
citizen_questions.a: A medical allowance of up to ₱7,000 a year for HMO-type benefits (Section 45), and for government lawyers a special counsel allowance of ₱5,000 for each court appearance, capped at 50% of the lawyer's monthly basic salary and never payable for appearances before quasi-judicial or administrative agencies (Section 47). PERA stayed at ₱2,000 a month and the net take-home pay floor at ₱5,000, unchanged since FY 2020.

citizen_questions.q: Can the government invest money it is not using?
citizen_questions.a: Yes, from this budget onward. Section 10 authorises the Chief Minister, on the finance minister's recommendation, to invest idle funds in excess of normal operating requirements in treasury bills through the Bureau of the Treasury — subject to Parliament's approval through the Committee on Finance, Budget and Management, with a quarterly report due within 7 days of each quarter's end.

citizen_questions.q: Can money be held back from a ministry?
citizen_questions.a: No. Section 54 provides that “no retention or deduction as reserves or overhead shall be made, except as authorized by law, the general or special provisions in this Act”. Earlier budgets carried a section with a similar heading but no such sentence; this is the first Bangsamoro budget in which the prohibition is actually stated.

citizen_questions.q: Could I see proof that a project was built?
citizen_questions.a: Section 73 required agencies to publish each project's title, location, description, cost estimates, winning contractor and bid within 30 calendar days of signing the contract, and the detailed actual cost and any variation orders within 30 calendar days of the certificate of completion. It also directed the Regional Project Monitoring and Evaluation Committee to require reporting of status and percentage of completion on an official website that every agency must establish and maintain.

citizen_questions.q: How long was the money available?
citizen_questions.a: Until 31 December 2026, with Personnel Services expiring 31 December 2025. Anything unreleased, unobligated, or obligated but not delivered by then reverts to the Bangsamoro Treasury for reappropriation. The constituent LGUs' share of taxes does not lapse at all.

display_header.what_this_does: Appropriates ₱94.41 billion for 2025 — the only regional budget smaller than the year before.

views.simple: The region's ₱94.41 billion budget for 2025 — 4.1% smaller than FY 2024, the only fall in the series — drawn from the block grant, other national subsidies, the region's share of national taxes collected in its territory, and “other revenues”. It funds 17 ministries, 11 other executive offices and 7 special purpose funds, including a Local Government Support Fund of ₱10.15 billion and two new funds for the Shari'ah courts and for Bangsamoro under special circumstances. Section 30 is the first Bangsamoro budget provision to address the Province of Sulu's departure, committing the government to keep implementing Sulu programmes and funding Sulu personnel while a Transition Plan is designed. Its 76 sections of operating rules add an idle-funds investment power, a medical allowance, a special counsel allowance for government lawyers, PhilGEPS as the primary procurement channel, and — for the first time — an express prohibition on retaining or deducting funds destined for ministries.
